title: Dielectric Properties and Microwave Reduction Behavior of BOF Slag and Lignin Mixture
abstract: Abstract Basic oxygen furnace (BOF) slag is the second highest byproduct generated in the European steel industry. In this study, the reduction behavior of BOF slag mixed with lignin, a byproduct of paper-pulp and bioethanol industries, under microwave heating was investigated. The microwave dielectric properties of a BOF slag-lignin mixture were measured under intense microwave electric fields. The microwave reduction experiments were carried out at 300 °C, 400 °C, 500 °C, 600 °C, 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C temperatures, for 10 minutes, under an inert N 2(g)  atmosphere. The microwave reduction results were compared with TGA reduction experiments conducted at the same temperatures. The dielectric properties showed that BOF slag can be heated under microwave efficiently due to its high permittivity and loss tangent values. The microwave reduction of BOF slag results indicated that increasing temperature leads to increase the reduction of srebrodolskite (main iron-bearing phase of BOF slag) to metallic iron, at 800 °C temperature, srebrodolskite completely reduced to iron metal under microwave energy. TGA results showed that srebrodolskite not fully reduced into iron metal event at 1000 °C. This indicates efficient reduction of BOF slag at lower temperature under microwave heating.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Basic oxygen furnace slag is a major byproduct of the steel industry, generated during the conversion of hot metal from blast furnace into steel in a basic oxygen furnace. In this method, hot metal is decarborized by blowing additional oxygen into the system, which removes carbon and other easily oxidized elements. BOF slag is the second highest generated byproduct in the steel industry, which is only less than blast furnace slag with, approximately 100–200 kg generated per ton of crude steel. [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 – 4 ]  This slag looks hard and wear-resistant due to its high iron content. [ 5 ]  The chemical composition of BOF slag mainly contains calcium, silicon, and iron oxides, which cover more than 80 pct of BOF slag elements. [ 6 ]  Among the mineral phases, the most prominent ones are portlandite, calcite, silicon oxide, periclase, and srebrodolskite. [ 7 , 8 ]  A significant amount vanadium is contained in BOF slag especially in Nordic region which comes from hot metal during the blast furnace process. [ 9 ]  Compared to blast furnace (BF) slag, basic oxygen furnace (BOF) slag exhibits lower grindability, with a grindability value of approximately 0.7. In contrast, BF slag has a higher value of about 0.96. [ 10 ]

Out of 16 million tons of the steel slag that is annually generated in Europe during the steel production, more than 50 pct will be BOF slag. [ 11 ]   Dumping these slag materials as waste poses serious environmental hazards due to the harmful compounds they contain and also leads to significant financial losses because of the valuable metals they hold. Unlike blast furnace slag, steel slag encounters technical difficulties in valorization, such as volume instability. [ 12 ]  Among the various applications, its use as raw material in road construction and the cement industry is the most common industrial approach. [ 11 , 13 ]  Naidu  et al . [ 14 ]  has explained that using BOF slag as a partial or complete substitute for cement binder benefits both waste recycling and reuse in the steel industry while enhancing the structural properties of cement and reducing its water demand. However, the residues left after iron recovery were significantly more reactive than raw BOF slag, making them suitable for use as a supplementary cementitious material during metallic iron recovery. [ 15 ]  Heidari  et al . [ 7 ]  also mentioned the challenges of using BOF slag as a construction material due to its silica content. Regarding the potential expansion and soundness issues caused by free calcium oxide in BOF slag, it is mandatory to evaluate the safety and sustainability of the steel slags before their use in the cement industry. [ 16 ]  Another steel slag recycling approach is hydrometallurgical extraction. Compared to the treatment of dust and sludge, the recovery of metals from slag using hydrometallurgical methods is generally more efficient due to the more stable phases and course particles. However, with the significant variations in the mineralogical composition of BOF slag, it is challenging to design a universal flowsheet with a standardized set of process conditions. [ 17 ]  Hydrolyzed lignin is used as the reducing agent. It is a complex, highly branched natural polymer and a major structural component of wood. [ 18 ]  This is the main byproduct of bioethanol, paper, and bio-oil industries. [ 19 ]  Using lignin as a reducing agent in the metallurgical industry will enable a net carbon-free process and address waste generation in the bioethanol industry.

Guo  et al . [ 15 ]  utilized BOF slag for iron recovery by mixing it with an additive-like mixture of carbon and kaolin-blended BOF slag to accelerate reduction reactions. The study further revealed that when basicity ranged from 0.97 to 1.31, the iron recovery percentage exceeded 95 pct. However, this addition results in the formation of a glassy phase, which hinders iron recovery from the slag by reducing the basicity of the mixture. Heidari  et al . [ 7 ]  studied the reduction behavior of BOF slag by using hydrogen. The results indicate that almost all the wüstite and srebrodolskite phases have been reduced into metallic iron at 900 °C. Using biomass as a potential reducing agent in steel byproduct valorization was also studied. Wang  et al . [ 20 ]  investigated the phosphorus removal from high-phosphorus steel slag by carbonized rice husk. Adding a carbonized rice husk equivalent to 3 carbon units and maintaining the temperature at 1500 °C for 30 minutes resulted in a 79.25 pct removal of P 2 O 5  from the slag. Further, Wei  et al . [ 21 ]  and Maduranga  et al . [ 22 ]  reported that biomass has the potential to reduce iron oxides under an inert atmosphere. Zuo  et al . [ 23 ]  concluded that biomass is a promising reductant for copper slag reduction, and that CaO addition can improve the reduction reaction. Attah-Kyei  et al . [ 24 ]  has demonstrated that biochar from biomass is a more effective reducing agent than coke for recovering valuable metals from nickel slag. Nevertheless, BOF slag reduction using biomass and microwave energy is an entirely novel concept that will enable a net-zero carbon valorization process. In this work hydrolysis lignin was used as the biomass which is the main byproduct in paper and pulp industry. Lignin comes from lignocellulosic biomass which has three main components called cellulose, hemi cellulose and lignin. Cellulose and hemicellulose are used in paper and pulp, and bioethanol industries where lignin remains as the major byproduct. In the present study, hydrolysis lignin was selected because of its low sulfur content. [ 22 ]  Currently, lignin is not widely utilized in high-value industrial applications, and large quantities are often disposed of or used for low-value purposes such as combustion. However, lignin contains a significant amount of fixed carbon, which makes it a promising candidate as a reducing agent in metallurgical processes.

In this study, microwave energy was utilized as a heating source. Microwave is an electromagnetic wave that contains both electric and magnetic fields with 1 to 1000 mm wavelengths. [ 25 ]  This direct energy transfer mechanism enables microwave heating to achieve significantly higher heat efficiency than conventional heating methods. In recent years, the use of microwave energy has shifted from food processing to advanced high-temperature material in fields such as mineral processing, organic synthesis, material preparation, steel and ceramic industries. [ 26 ,  27 ,  28 ,  29 – 30 ]  This microwave energy has been successfully used in the steel waste recycling areas, Omran  et al . [ 31 ]  reported a successful zinc removal from EAF dust using microwave heating. Further, Omran  et al . [ 32 ]  reported an improvement in phosphorus removal from iron ore using combined microwave pretreatment and ultrasonic treatment.

Microwave heating operates by inducing dielectric losses within the material, whereby the absorbed microwave energy is directly transferred to the internal molecules or atoms involved in the reaction. This direct energy transfer mechanism enables microwave heating to achieve significantly higher heat efficiency compared to conventional heating methods. [ 33 , 34 ]  The iron-bearing oxides in the BOF slag exhibit efficient microwave-absorptive properties, making them a good candidate for rapid heating during the reduction process. [ 35 ]  In addition to the material’s dielectric properties, factors such as microwave frequency, temperature, moisture content, and chemical composition also influence the efficiency of microwave absorption.

In this work, the dielectric properties of raw BOF slag and a BOF slag-lignin mixture were analyzed using a dual-mode microwave cavity, which allows simultaneous heating and cavity-perturbation dielectric measurements within the same microwave frequency range. The microwave reduction behavior of BOF slag and lignin mixture were carried out by using microwave device with 2.45 GHz frequency and 4 kW power intensity. The reduction experiments were carried out in at 300 °C, 400 °C, 500 °C, 600 °C, 700 °C, 800 °C and 900 °C temperatures range for 10 minutes. The same reduction experiments were carried out with TGA at the same temperatures and compared with microwave reduction experiments.

sections.heading: Materials
Microwave Reduction Experiments
paragraphs: Dielectric properties were measured using a dual-mode cylindrical microwave cavity operating under the cavity-perturbation method (CPM), which enables  in situ , real-time permittivity determination during microwave heating. The setup employs two independently coupled ports: a high-power heating channel and a low-power measurement channel. In the heating channel, the RF signal (swept around the resonance) is generated and then amplified to deliver up to ~ 150 W to the cavity. A power isolator with a matched (dummy) load absorbs reflected power to protect the amplifier, while a directional coupler allows forward and reflected power to be monitored independently. Heating power is coupled through an electric probe on the cavity side wall (N-type port) that excites a mode resonant near the ISM band (~ 2.45 GHz).

For dielectric characterization, a second probe excites a distinct cavity mode at a lower frequency (~ 2.1–2.2 GHz), coupled through the bottom wall (SMA port). High isolation between heating and measurement channels is ensured by the dual-mode design and filtering, allowing resonance tracking (frequency and Q-factor) in the measurement mode while heating proceeds. Temperature is typically monitored non-contact ( e.g. , IR pyrometry) through an access aperture, and the cavity can be stabilized ( e.g. , water cooling) to minimize drift. A detailed description of the cavity design, instrumentation, isolation strategy, and measurement procedure is given by. [ 36 ]
The microwave reduction was conducted using a 2.45 GHz microwave oven with a maximum output power of 4 kW, as shown in Figure  1 . Fig. 1 Microwave setup for the experiment from Reference  37

The samples were contained in a microwave-transparent alumina crucible embedded in an alumina refractory block of the same transparency. Then the refractory block was carefully placed at the center of the microwave furnace on a low-density porous alumina support to ensure stable positioning and uniform heating. Nitrogen gas was used to maintain the inert atmosphere throughout the experiment, as shown in Figure  1 . Volatile materials were collected on filter paper. The experiments were conducted at different temperatures of 300 °C, 400 °C, 500 °C, 600 °C, 700 °C, 800 °C and 900 °C for 10 minutes under an inert atmosphere. In addition, dynamic experiments were carried out without setting the temperature of the reduction.

sections.heading: TGA Experiments
paragraphs: Conventional thermal reduction experiment was conducted by thermogravimetric analysis (TG) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) using a NETZSCH STA 449 F3 system integrated with a graphite furnace which is capable to analysis both mass reduction and heat flow changes at the same time. The volatile-gas outlet of the apparatus was connected to a NETZSCH QMS 403 D mass spectrometer (NETZSCH, Selb, Germany), which facilitated  in situ  monitoring and identification of gaseous species evolved throughout the thermogravimetric (TG) analysis. Combining TGA analysis with differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and mass spectrometry (MS) provides complementary information for interpreting thermal analysis. During the study, a fixed heating rate is supplied to the furnace (10 °C/min), where the heat flow will be continuously monitored by the DSC instrument by considering the temperature change inside the stove, hence defining whether the reaction is endothermic or exothermic. At the same time, volatile components are directly transferred into the mass spectrometer and identified by analyzing ionic current fluctuations. All the experiments were conducted under an inert atmosphere. The reduction experiment was carried out in the TG furnace under isothermal temperature of 700 °C, 800 °C, 1000 °C, and 1200 °C for 100 minutes.

sections.heading: Equilibrium Composition
paragraphs: The equilibrium composition was calculated with FactSage 8.3 to determine the thermodynamic behavior of the reduction process. Since most of the mineral phases are oxides, the FToxid database was used in conjunction with the FactPS database to assess the presence of lignin, which contains fixed carbon. All the solid solutions and gas phases were considered including monoxides, spinels and slag phases. All calculations were done under an inert (N 2(g) ) atmosphere.

sections.heading: Characterization of Materials
paragraphs: The mineral phases and crystal structures were identified by using a Rigaku MiniFlex 600 C X Ray X-ray diffractometer with a Co source at the Centre for Material Analysis at the University of Oulu. The diffraction patterns were analyzed using Rigaku’s PDXL 2.6 software for X-ray powder diffraction, and the phases were identified based on reference data from the ICDD PDF-4 database. The chemical composition of BOF slag was determined with PANalytical Axios max 4 kW XRF machine (Malvern Panalytical, Almelo, The Netherlands). A Zeiss ULTRA Plus field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM), coupled with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) system, was used to examine the microstructural and elemental composition of residues from various mixtures.

sections.heading: Characterization of Raw BOF Slag and Lignin
paragraphs: The chemical and mineralogical composition, as well as micromorphological properties of raw BOF slag and lignin were identified by using XRF, XRD, and SEM-EDX analysis. The chemical composition is shown in Table  II . Table II Chemical Analysis of BOF Slag Element FeO V 2 O 3 MnO Cr 2 O 3 MgO CaO SiO 2 TiO 2 Al 2 O 3 Conc. (Pct) 17.4 3.13 2.31 0.27 1.46 44.8 11.3 1.13 1.32

The chemical composition shows a significant concentration of iron oxides in the BOF slag, highlighting the relevance of this study in reducing iron oxides to metallic iron. In addition to iron oxide, vanadium (V), chromium (Cr), magnesium (Mg), calcium (Ca) and manganese (Mn) are also detected as metal oxides during the XRF analysis. A higher concentration of oxygen and calcium indicates that these other elements can exist as calcium oxide spinel structures in BOF slag. [ 38 ]  The XRD analysis is presented in Figure  2 . The analysis indicates that the primary iron-bearing compound in the sample is srebrodolskite (Ca 2 Fe 2 O 5 ). Additionally, minor compounds such as hematite (Fe 2 O 3 ), magnetite (Fe 3 O 4 ), wüstite (FeO), and metallic iron (Fe) are also present in the sample. Furthermore, portlandite (Ca(OH) 2 ), calcite (CaCO 3 ), and quartz (SiO 2 ) were identified during the XRD analysis of the raw BOF slag. Fig. 2 XRD analysis of raw BOF slag

According to slag chemistry, the coexistence of lime and quartz as separate compounds is unusual due to the high basicity of BOF slag (NBO/Si ≈ 4), [ 39 ]  the silicate structure is expected to consist primarily of isolated tetrahedra. This phenomenon is also confirmed by Belhadj  et al . [ 6 ]  and [ 40 ]  who, revealed the presence of  β  – dicalcium silicate in their samples. However, several other studies have also reported lime and quartz as distinct mineral phases, including those by. [ 7 , 41 ]  Generally, two types of solid solutions are also mentioned in literature, wüstite and lime-rich alloy mixtures. [ 42 ]

As shown in Figure  3 , the EDX point analysis of raw BOF slag indicates the main phase is srebrodolskite. Other than that, metallic iron, calcium silicate, and wüstite can also be seen from the SEM-EDX point analysis. Fig. 3 SEM image of raw BOF slag

Based on the EDX data, the following observations can be made. Within the calcium silicate phase, EDX point analysis revealed a Ca:Si ratio of approximately 3, indicating a higher calcium content relative to silicon. This composition suggests the crystal structure corresponds to  β –dicalcium silicate or isolated tetrahedra, as previously reported by Chaurand  et al . [ 43 ]  Regions identified as wüstite were found to contain solid solutions enriched in Fe, Ca, Mn, and Al, however, these were predominantly composed of Fe and O, supporting their classification as (Fe, Ca, Mn, Al) O-type solid solutions. In contrast to some literature reports, lime-rich alloyed phases could not be distinctly identified in the sample studied. Additionally, metallic iron was observed to be surrounded by the srebrodolskite phase, and vanadium was frequently detected in association with the dicalcium silicate phase.

Lignin was utilized as the reducing agent for the reduction of BOF slag. The lignin used in this experiment is the same sample referenced in our previous study [ 22 ]  which has 28.9 pct fixed carbon. As shown in Figure  4 (a), SEM images of raw lignin reveal high porosity, reflecting its volatility and heterogeneity, with irregular branches. Unlike raw lignin, pyrolyzed lignin, shown in Figure  4 (b), has become a denser and brittle material with the removal of volatile matter from the sample, as well as the accumulation of fixed carbon inside the sample. Fig. 4 SEM images of lignin ( a ) before pyrolysis, ( b ) after pyrolysis

sections.heading: Gibbs Free Energy Calculation and Equilibrium Composition
paragraphs: The Gibbs free energy and equilibrium amounts were calculated before the experiment, as shown in Figures  5 (a) and (b), respectively. Factsage 8.3 thermodynamic software was used to obtain the results. These Gibbs free energy values indicate the spontaneity of the reduction of srebrodolskite to metallic iron at different temperatures when using fixed carbon as a reducing agent. As shown in Figure  5 (a), around 800 °C, srebrodolskite can be reduced into metallic iron with adequate fixed carbon. In our study, the experimental temperature range was 300 °C to 900 °C to determine how well the reduction reaction occurred across different temperature regions. Fig. 5 Thermodynamics interpretation of BOF slag reduction: ( a ) Gibbs free energy calculation of srebrodolskite reduction reaction, ( b ) Equilibrium composition of BOF slag + C mixture

An equilibrium analysis of BOF slag reduction with biomass (fixed carbon) was conducted until the temperature reached 1200 °C. The findings indicate that the fixed carbon in the biomass has been sufficient for the complete reduction of srebrodolskite to metallic iron in an inert atmosphere. Notably, the reduction of srebrodolskite has started around 300 °C where, CaO (s)  has become CaCO 3(s) . This transformation likely resulted from the formation of CO 2(g)  due to the oxidation of fixed carbon during the reduction of iron oxides, which subsequently combined with CaO (s)  to form CaCO 3(s)  at lower temperatures. [ 44 ]  As the temperature reached approximately 575 °C, CaCO 3(s)  completely decomposed into carbonates, reforming CaO (s) . However, the equilibrium analysis assumes an infinite time frame, focusing on Gibbs free energy minimization rather than reaction kinetics; in practice, this may yield slightly different results. Nonetheless, reducing iron oxides to metallic iron can be effectively achieved using this process, as shown in the Factsage results.

sections.heading: Thermal Analysis of BOF Slag and Lignin Mixture
paragraphs: The thermal analysis of the powder mixture was performed using TG, DSC, and MS, as shown in Figure  6 . The mass curve shows a more than 20 pct loss in mass after the experiment in inert atmosphere. Fig. 6 Thermal analysis of BOF and lignin mixture under inert (N 2(g) ) atmosphere: ( a ) TG analysis; ( b ) DSC analysis; ( c ) mass spectrometry analysis

In the temperature range of 0 °C to 200 °C, a mass loss of 1.03 pct was observed in the TG curve, accompanied by the release of H 2 O (g)  in the mass spectrometry data, indicating the evaporation of physically adsorbed moisture from the BOF slag and lignin. The corresponding endothermic heat consumption was 139.8 J/g, as shown in the DSC curve. XRD analysis of the raw BOF slag confirmed the presence of portlandite and calcite phases. Correspondingly, the thermal analysis shows endothermic peaks associated with the dihydroxylation of portlandite between 430 °C and 500 °C, and the decomposition of carbonates and reduction of iron oxides between 640 °C and 770 °C, [ 31 ]  with enthalpy changes of 36.9 and 36.8 J/g, respectively. At this temperature, the conversion of calcite to lime is also evident in the FactSage results. These observations are further supported by mass spectrometry data, which show variations in the ion current signals for H 2 O (g)  and CO 2 (g) , as illustrated in Figure  6 . Furthermore, the FactSage results indicate a complete reduction of calcium ferrite at 320 °C, which is unrealistic under practical conditions, where reaction kinetics and time constraints play major roles in the reduction process. An exothermic peak with an enthalpy changes of 47.2 J/g was observed between 500 °C and 640 °C, which can be aligned with char formation. Similar behavior was reported by Huang  et al ., [ 45 ]  by mentioning this exothermic event with the recombination of chemical bonds during the coke formation process, leading to the release of energy. Between 880 °C and 1100 °C, a mass loss of 2.69 pct was observed, accompanied by a broad endothermic peak with an enthalpy change of 24.6 J/g.

sections.heading: Dielectric Properties of Raw BOF Slag and BOF Slag – Lignin Mixture
paragraphs: The dielectric properties of raw BOF slag and the BOF slag-lignin mixture are presented in Figure  7 . As shown in Figure  7 (a), the BOF slag-lignin mixture exhibits lower microwave absorbance compared to raw BOF slag. This is attributed to the dilution of iron oxides within the mixture, which decreases the sample’s conductivity loss relative to the raw BOS slag. Additionally, lignin acts as an insulating layer between iron oxide phases in the initial stage, controlling or hindering permittivity. [ 46 ] Fig. 7 Dielectric properties of raw BOF slag and BOF slag – lignin mixture; ( a ) real permittivity, ( b ) imaginary permittivity, ( c ) loss tangent

However, the loss factor shown in Figure  7 (b) (imaginary permittivity) increases significantly in the mixture. The thermal analysis of the BOF slag-lignin mixture indicates that the pyrolysis process occurs around 600 °C. Above 600 °C, the loss factor increases rapidly in the mixture, due to the formation of biochar, which leads to interfacial polarization between carbon and the iron oxide phase, thereby increasing the overall loss factor of the sample. [ 47 ]  The loss factor continuously increases to 800 °C for the mixture, then declines, which should mark the completion of iron oxide reduction to metallic iron according to the thermal analysis results. However, there was no drop in the loss factor in raw BOF samples, indicating that the unreduced iron oxides continuously convert electricity into heat. The loss tangent of the raw BOF slag and the slag/lignin mixture in Figure  7 (c) indicates how efficiently microwave energy is converted into heat. The results show that the slag/lignin mixture exhibits increasingly rapid heating, particularly above 600 °C, when lignin is pyrolyzed into biochar. This enhanced dielectric loss continues until the iron oxides in the slag are fully reduced to metallic iron at approximately 800 °C.

sections.heading: Microwave Reduction of BOF Slag/Lignin Mixture
Microwave reduction of BOF slag/lignin briquettes
paragraphs: As shown in Table  I , the briquettes were reduced isothermally for 10 minutes at different temperatures ranging from 300 °C to 900 °C. The results are shown in Figures  8 , and  9 . Figure  8  shows the mineral phases of reduced samples at 300 °C, 400 °C, 500 °C, and 600 °C. Compared to the raw BOF samples, the peak patterns at 300 °C and 400 °C show very similar behavior. This indicates that the reduction process has not yet begun, despite the thermodynamic calculations suggesting the onset of reducing srebrodolskite to metallic iron around 320 °C. At 300 °C, both portlandite and calcite can be observed, but they are no longer present after 500 °C, where only lime is detectable. This change may be attributed to the dihydroxylation and decomposition of carbonates and hydroxides as explained in thermal analysis. Fig. 8 XRD results of reduced briquettes samples at 300  ° C, 400  ° C, and 500  ° C for 10 mins under microwave heating Fig. 9 XRD results of reduced briquettes samples at 700  ° C, 800  ° C, and 900  ° C for 10 mins under microwave heating

At 500 °C, reduction processes begin, leading to the disappearance of the wüstite phase from the peak patterns, as illustrated in Figure  8 . This phenomenon is confirmed by Romanov  et al . [ 48 ]  by mentioning that wüstite can be observed below 302 °C or above 570 °C. However, Chaurand  et al . [ 43 ]  reported that the reduction of calcium ferrite does not begin until1090 K (817 °C) in hydrogen atmosphere. Similarly, Li  et al . [ 28 ]  reported that carbon monoxide (CO) detected by mass spectrometry indicates that calcium ferrite reduction initiates only above 1250 K (977 °C) during carbothermic reduction. In contrast, under microwave heating at 700 °C, most of the iron oxides in calcium ferrites are reduced to metallic iron, as shown in the XRD results in Figure  9 , peak intensity of metallic iron has been increased. The presence of larnite indicates the agglomeration of lime with silica, resulting in the reformation of calcium silicate, probably with an isolated tetrahedral crystal structure. At temperature of 800 °C, no calcium ferrite phase can be detected, indicating that the srebrodolskite phase has been successfully reduced to metallic iron using lignin under microwave radiation. By 900 °C, neither iron oxides nor calcium ferrite can be observed; instead, only metallic iron is present as the iron-bearing phase.

SEM-EDX analysis was conducted on each sample to verify the XRD results and obtain morphological features. The results are presented in Figures  10  and  12 . As shown in Figure  10 (a), the main phases for the sample heated at 300 °C are S1-S5 listed in Table  III . Based on the elemental compositions identified in each spectrum, the phases are as follows: S1 and S3 consist of metallic iron, S2 is calcium silicate, S4 contains wüstite agglomerated with magnesium and manganese oxides, and S5 is calcium ferrite (srebrodolskite). These phases align perfectly with the XRD results shown in Figure  8 . From the SEM images, it is clearly visible that the darkest regions indicate calcium silicate, while the brightest regions represent metallic iron. Since backscattered electrons were used for characterization, the heaviest compounds appear the brightest. [ 49 ]  The metallic iron phase is covered by slightly less bright grains of wüstite, followed by the third brightest grains of calcium ferrite. A similar behavior is observed at 400 °C, as illustrated in Figure  10 (b). The main difference at this temperature is the enlargement of the metallic iron phase and the absence of wüstite, suggesting that wüstite is reduced even at lower temperatures. However, the calcium ferrite phase remains unchanged. Notably, iron oxide predominantly forms as calcium-manganese-iron oxide at these temperatures (S9). In Figures  10 (c) and (d), an increase in metallic iron content is evident, especially in Figure  10 (d), where the reduction process of calcium ferrite has begun. Despite this, a significant amount of calcium ferrite phases containing iron oxides remains. Additionally, vanadium has combined with calcium silicate at these temperatures, as shown in S13, where it has been identified in the XRD results as calcium vanadyl oxide. At 400 °C, the propagation of thermal cracks is clearly visible. Under microwave radiation, different mineral grains heat at different rates due to their dielectric properties. Therefore, the larger thermal deformation of one mineral phase is constrained by the other minerals, generating thermal stress and hence crack propagation. In tension, once a single crack is generated, it would accelerate throughout the sample leading to failure. [ 50 ]  Moreover, the metallic iron phases are enveloped by a calcium iron oxide matrix, with a thin wüstite layer observed between them. This microstructural feature clearly indicates the ongoing reduction of calcium iron oxide to metallic iron. Apart from the SEM images, the surface of each briquette at 300 °C to 600 °C is shown in Figure  11 . It clearly shows that as the temperature increases, the heat distribution becomes well distributed throughout the sample. At 300 °C and 400 °C, unburnt lignin can be seen in several areas of the surface. By increasing the temperature to 500 °C and 600 °C, the heat distribution improved and there was no sign of unburnt lignin on the surface. Fig. 11 Microwave heating of the briquettes at 300 °C, 400 °C, 500 °C, and 600 °C temperatures

Further reduction of calcium ferrite was observed at higher temperatures, as shown in Figure  12 . In Figure  12 (a), a higher amount of metallic iron is present at 700 °C compared to 600 °C; however, some calcium ferrite phases can still be detected, as indicated by S17, S18, and S20 in Table  III . At this temperature, the highest concentration of vanadium is observed alongside calcium and oxygen (S21), which XRD results identify as calcium vanadate in Figure  9 (a). Unreduced iron oxides are present as calcium-manganese-iron oxide and calcium-magnesium-iron silicate phases, with higher grain sizes indicating a remaining kinetic barrier at this temperature range. At 800 °C, a 10-minute heat treatment is sufficient for the complete reduction of calcium ferrite to metallic iron under microwave heating, as no iron-bearing phases remain except for metallic iron at this temperature, according to SEM-EDX and XRD results. This indicates a complete reduction of BOF slag with lignin in an inert atmosphere. The conditions remained consistent even at 900 °C, further confirming that the optimum temperature for reducing srebrodolskite to metallic iron is 800 °C. Fig. 12 SEM images of briquettes after microwave heating: ( a ) 10 mins at 700 °C, ( b ) 10 mins at 800 °C, ( c ) 10 mins at 900  ° C

Furthermore, the briquettes after the microwave reduction at 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C are shown in Figure  13 . It is clearly visible that sintering of the surface occurs at 800 °C and 900 °C. Since the unburnt lignin has been disappeared in the surface of briquettes, indicated that the lignin has been fully utilized in the reduction process. Fig. 13 Microwave heating of the briquettes at 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C temperatures

The semi-quantification analysis of XRD results for briquettes reduced under microwave heating at different temperatures was performed using the Rietveld method to assess the extent of phase transformation at each temperature as shown in Table  IV . The results showed that, at 300 °C, Srebrodolskite (calcium ferrite) has the highest iron content. With increasing temperature, the calcium ferrite content gradually reduced while calcium silicate and calcium-manganese oxide phases contents increased at higher temperatures. At 800 °C, the iron oxide bearing phases, including Srebrodolskite and calcium iron oxide have been fully reduced to metallic iron. sections.heading: Microwave reduction of BOF slag/lignin powder
paragraphs: This work aims to investigate the effect of using briquetted versus powder samples on the efficiency of microwave reduction of BOF slag. The same experimental conditions were applied to BOF slag and lignin mixture samples, tested as powders, at temperatures ranging from 700 °C to 900 °C. The goal was to compare the results with those of the briquette samples to identify which form would be more efficient for the reduction process.

The XRD results at 700 °C, shown in Figure  14 , clearly indicate the presence of unreduced srebrodolskite in the sample, and iron oxide was not presented as srebrodolskite. In addition to srebrodolskite, other iron-bearing phases, such as calcium iron oxide, calcium-manganese-iron oxide, and metallic iron, were also identified. Iron oxide remains in the calcium-manganese-iron oxide phase at 800 °C, which was not detected in the briquette samples. Fig. 14 XRD of the reduced powder samples at 700, 800, 900  ° C for 10 mins under microwave heating

This suggests that complete reduction of the powder samples has not been achieved even at 900 °C, unlike the briquette samples, which showed complete reduction at 800 °C. This is an interesting observation as the pellets slow the reaction rate under conventional heating due to their higher compaction and denser structure compared to powder samples. Moreover, it hinders the gasification of fixed carbon into CO (g)  due to high activation energy inside the micro pellets. [ 51 ]  However, under the microwave radiation, pellets being denser can absorb microwaves more effectively and heat more uniformly. Fine powder, on the other hand, often reflects or scatters microwaves and can have poor particle to particle contact, leading to uneven heating and localized hot spots. [ 52 ]  In micro pellets, carbon and iron oxide are closely packed, ensuring good solid–solid contact. [ 53 ]  Therefore, under microwave heating, it is possible to achieve a faster reduction rate in briquettes than in powder samples.

SEM-EDX analysis was conducted to examine the microstructure of the powder samples, thus confirming the results obtained from the XRD analysis. The EDX analysis at 700 °C, as shown in Figure  15 (a) and Table  V , provides clear evidence of the presence of calcium iron oxide and wüstite in samples S35, S36, and S39, indicating incomplete reduction at this temperature. The analysis of powder samples at 800 °C, illustrated in Figure  15 (b), revealed the presence of calcium-manganese-iron oxide (sample S41), which aligns perfectly with the XRD results. Notably, this compound was not observed in the same briquette sample. This finding leads us to conclude that 800 °C for 10 minutes is sufficient for the briquette to achieve complete reduction; however, it is inadequate for the powder samples. Even when the temperature was increased, as shown in Figure  15 (c), wüstite, calcium iron oxide, and calcium iron manganese oxides were still present in the samples at 900 °C. Similar to the briquette samples, a significant amount of vanadium was detected in the calcium silicate phase (samples S37, S38, and S51). Another important observation was the clear visibility of sintering in the powder sample at 900 °C, marked as A1 in Figure  15 (c). sections.heading: TG Reduction of BOF/Lignin Mixture
paragraphs: To evaluate the microwave reduction efficiency compared to conventional thermal reduction, TG reduction experiments were carried out under the same temperature and atmosphere conditions. The TG reduction tests were conducted for 100 minutes at each temperature, whereas microwave reduction was conducted for only 10 minutes. Afterward, the residues were analyzed using XRD and SEM-EDX to determine the final composition of the samples. The XRD results for the reduced powder samples are displayed in Figure  16 . Fig. 16 XRD of TG reduced BOF powder samples for 100 mins at 700 °C, 1000 °C, 1200 °C

The XRD results indicate the presence of more srebrodolskite and calcium ferrite phases at 700 °C, which suggests minimal reduction at this temperature. Significant intensity of calcium iron ferrite was also observed at heating temperatures of 1000 °C. This indicates that the 100 minutes of TG reduction was insufficient to achieve complete reduction of iron-bearing phases into iron metal, whereas the briquettes were completely reduced in 10 minutes with microwave reduction. This indicates the catalytic effect of microwave energy in enhancing the carbothermic reduction rate. [ 54 ]  Because microwave heating occurs within the material, highly microwave-absorbing compounds such as iron oxides heat much faster than the surrounding phases. This rapid, localized heating generates thermal stresses that cause microcracks to form within the iron oxide grains. These cracks enhance the diffusion of reducing gases into the particle interior, thereby promoting faster reduction. This is clearly evident in the SEM image shown in Figure  16 , where microcracks have propagated through the calcium ferrite phase, while the calcium silicate phase remains undisturbed. [ 55 , 56 ]

At 1200 °C, analysis of both XRD and SEM-EDX results showed that calcium iron ferrite was no longer present in the residues, indicating complete reduction of iron oxides had been achieved. Additionally, the results showed that vanadium exists as calcium vanadium silicate within the calcium silicate phase. As the heating temperature increased, iron from the calcium-manganese-iron oxide phase was removed and reduced, while manganese oxide remained in the residues (Figure  17 ). Fig. 17 Thermal cracks propagating on the calcium ferrite phase could lead to a localized, rapid reduction

The XRD results were verified using SEM-EDX data, as shown in Figure  18 . The spectrum results aligned perfectly with the XRD phases. In Figure  18 (a), at 700 °C, a higher amount of the metallic iron phase (S61) was observed; however, the wüstite phase (S66) remained clearly visible, indicating the ongoing reduction process. Additionally, S64 and S66 showed a high concentration of calcium ferrite, suggesting the presence of unreduced iron oxides in the sample. According to the SEM images presented in Figures  18 (b) and (c), taken at 800 °C and 900 °C, respectively, wüstite phase has disappeared from the system, although calcium ferrite remained (S70 and S73). This phase was not detectable under microwave heating after reaching 700 °C for briquettes. Furthermore, calcium-manganese-iron oxide was identified in S69. Finally, at 1200 °C, as shown in Figure  18 (d), there was no sign of calcium ferrite or calcium-manganese-iron oxide. Instead, metallic iron was formed on a larger scale, indicating the complete reduction of iron oxides to metallic iron under conventional heating at this temperature within 100 minutes. Additionally, a significantly higher presence of vanadium in the form of calcium vanadium silicate was observed at 900 °C (S74 and S75), suggesting that this temperature may be optimal for agglomerating vanadium into the calcium silicate phase. Fig. 18 SEM images of TG reduced BOF powder samples for 100 mins: ( a ) at 700 °C, ( b ) at 800 °C, ( c ) at 1000 °C, ( d ) at 1200 °C

The semi-quantification analysis of XRD results for the samples reduced with TG are shown in Table  VIII . The results revealed that there is no significant reduction occurring at 700 °C, By increased the temperature to 1000 °C, the reduction degree increased and a fully reduction has been occurred at 1200 °C where it was achieved at 800 °C under microwave heating. sections.heading: Process Evaluation and Industrial Application
paragraphs: Microwave energy used as a heating source could be more efficient compared to the conventional heating. Microwave energy has several advantages compared with conventional heating methods, particularly in metallurgical and materials processing applications. Unlike conventional furnaces that rely on heat transfer from external sources, microwave heating enables volumetric and selective heating of materials, which can significantly reduce processing time and overall energy consumption. In the present study, the direct interaction of microwave energy with the BOF slag creates rapid heating and improving metal recovery efficiency while lowering thermal losses. Previous studies have reported that microwave-assisted processes may achieve higher energy efficiency due to reduced heat dissipation to furnace walls and shorter treatment durations. [ 57 , 58 ]

From an industrial perspective, microwave technology has already been explored in several large-scale material processing applications, including mineral treatment, waste valorization, and metallurgical extraction. However, several challenges remain for full industrial implementation. These include the relatively high capital cost of industrial microwave generators, potential non-uniform heating at larger scales, and the need for optimized reactor designs to ensure efficient coupling between microwave energy and the processed material. Additionally, the dielectric properties of the slag materials can be changed due to the significant fluctuation of iron oxides inside the slag, which must be carefully considered when designing large-scale systems. Apart from these challenges, the rapid heating rates, potential reductions in energy consumption, and improved process selectivity suggest that microwave-assisted processing represents a promising alternative to conventional thermal treatments.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study aims to investigate the reduction behavior of BOF slag and lignin under microwave energy in inert atmosphere. The main conclusions are: The dielectric properties of the BOF slag/lignin mixture are governed mainly by iron oxide content, transformation of lignin into biochar, and phase transformation occurred during the reduction progress. At low temperatures, BOF slag shows a good microwave absorbance compared to BOF/lignin mixture owing to the dilution of iron oxides and the insulating effect of lignin, which lowers conductivity loss. Above ~ 600 °C, lignin pyrolysis produces biochar, which significantly increasing the loss factor of the BOF slag/lignin through enhanced interfacial polarization between carbon and iron oxide phases, leading to more efficient microwave heating. This effect continues until about 800 °C, where a decline in the loss factor indicates the completion of iron oxide reduction to metallic iron. Microwave reduction experiments indicated that a complete reduction of iron oxides in the BOF slag into iron metal can be achieved at 800 °C with 10 minutes of isothermal reduction of the BOF slag/lignin briquettes. The results showed that the pellets exhibited efficient and higher degree of reduction under microwave heating compared to powder samples, due to their compact structure enhanced the heating rate of iron oxide through more efficient microwave absorption TG reduction experiments showed that BOF slag/lignin mixture did not achieve a fully reduction of iron-bearing phases into iron metal even at 1000 °C. This indicates the reduction capability of BOF slag/lignin at lower temperature under microwave heating Further investigation is still required, particularly regarding the use of hydrogen rather than biomass in the microwave-assisted reduction process. Future studies could also explore initiating the reduction with hydrogen and subsequently switching to carbon to achieve optimal reduction efficiency. Additionally, methods for extracting vanadium from the calcium silicate phase need to be developed.
